His coach approached moments later and knelt down to his level, reminding him that the team had made it to the championship for the first time in eight years specifically because of improvements Diego had made all season, missed shot included. He pointed out that even professional players missed important shots sometimes, and that what defined a player was not one missed moment but how they chose to keep showing up afterward. Diego felt the heavy sadness in his chest shift slightly, making room for something steadier and more hopeful as he considered his coach's words seriously for the first time since the final whistle. By the time he climbed into the car beside his sister's proud, crayon-covered poster, a small, determined hope had begun replacing his despair, a quiet certainty that next season would bring another chance, and that he intended to be ready for it.

prompt: Write a story about a girl recovering from illness who feels lonely and then becomes joyful.
response: Simone lay propped against pillows in her bed, staring at the same ceiling she had been staring at for nearly three weeks straight while recovering from a long illness that had kept her home from school and away from all her usual activities. The house felt unbearably quiet during the day while her parents worked and her older brother attended school, leaving her alone with nothing but television reruns and the occasional phone call from a friend who always seemed to be in a hurry to get back to their own normal, busy life. She missed the noisy chaos of the school cafeteria, missed passing notes in class, missed simply existing among other people instead of this endless, isolated quiet that had become her entire world. Her friends had stopped by once during the first week, but visits grew less frequent as the weeks dragged on, everyone else's lives moving forward while hers remained frozen in this same bedroom, day after identical day. She scrolled through photos on her phone of her friends at a birthday party she had missed, a loneliness settling deep in her chest at seeing everyone laughing together without her, as if the world had simply continued on without noticing her absence at all. She stopped responding to group chat messages some days, finding it too painful to read about activities and plans she could not be part of while stuck recovering at home. The isolation wore on her more than the illness itself had, each quiet, friendless afternoon stretching longer than the last, until she genuinely wondered if her friends would forget about her entirely by the time she finally returned to school. One Saturday afternoon, as she lay listlessly watching another rerun, she heard an unusual commotion outside her window, voices and laughter drifting up from the front yard. Confused, she pulled herself out of bed and peered outside to find nearly her entire class gathered on her lawn, holding up handmade signs and balloons, having organized a surprise outdoor visit specifically because they had missed her and wanted her to know it even though she could not go out and play with them directly. Her best friend held up a phone, suggesting they all video call together so Simone could join in from her window while everyone played games below that she could watch and laugh along with from a safe distance. Joy flooded through Simone so suddenly and completely that tears sprang to her eyes, the weeks of lonely isolation melting away as she waved down at the friends who had clearly been thinking about her the entire time. They stayed for nearly two hours, playing games just for her entertainment and shouting updates up to her window, and Simone laughed harder that afternoon than she had in weeks. By the time they finally left, promising to return again soon, the loneliness that had consumed her for weeks had been replaced entirely by a warm, grateful joy, certain now more than ever that she had never truly been forgotten at all.

prompt: Write a story about a cat who feels angry about a new kitten and then learns to feel calm.
response: Whiskers the cat glared from the top of the bookshelf, watching the tiny new kitten named Pip tumble playfully across the living room floor, batting at a toy mouse that used to be Whiskers' exclusive favorite before this intruder had arrived in the house just one week ago. Every time Whiskers' owner scooped up the kitten for cuddles, a hot, prickly anger flared in his chest, and he found himself hissing at Pip whenever the kitten dared to approach his favorite sunny windowsill or his usual spot on the couch cushion. He had been the only pet in the house for six years, and this sudden change felt like a betrayal he had never agreed to, his once peaceful territory now constantly invaded by a bouncing, mewing bundle of energy who seemed to have no concept of personal space whatsoever. Whiskers took to swatting Pip away whenever the kitten got too close, growling low warnings that only seemed to confuse the kitten rather than discourage him, since Pip simply bounced back moments later with the same relentless enthusiasm. His owner scolded him gently for the hissing, which only deepened Whiskers' frustration, feeling as though his own territory and his own family had suddenly turned against him in favor of this newcomer. He spent most days now perched high on the bookshelf, refusing to come down even for his usual favorite spots, nursing his anger in isolated, grumpy solitude. One rainy afternoon, a sudden loud crash of thunder sent Pip scrambling in terror beneath the couch, where he remained stuck, too frightened to move, his small cries of distress growing increasingly desperate as the storm continued outside. Whiskers, still perched high on his bookshelf, found himself watching the kitten's obvious fear with something unexpected stirring beneath his anger, a flicker of old memory about how frightening his own first thunderstorm had felt as a tiny kitten many years before. Against his own stubborn resistance, he found himself climbing down and approaching the couch, peering underneath at Pip's trembling, terrified form. Something in Whiskers softened at the sight, and he squeezed beneath the couch himself, settling his larger body protectively beside the frightened kitten until Pip's trembling slowly eased against his warm fur. They remained like that until the storm passed completely, and when Whiskers' owner found them curled together beneath the couch afterward, she smiled warmly, scratching them both behind the ears. Whiskers realized, in that quiet moment, that his anger over the past week had cost him more peace than Pip's clumsy enthusiasm ever actually had. The tight, hot anger that had gripped him for days finally dissolved into a calm, settled acceptance, and from that afternoon forward, Whiskers allowed Pip to share his sunny windowsill, discovering that the company was actually rather pleasant once he stopped resisting it.

prompt: Write a story about a boy who feels nervous running his first lemonade stand and then feels proud.
response: Теодор arranged his pitcher of lemonade and stack of paper cups on the small folding table at the end of his driveway, glancing nervously up and down the empty street where not a single car or pedestrian had passed in nearly twenty minutes since he set everything up. He had spent his entire allowance on lemons, sugar, and cups, convinced this would be the summer he finally earned enough money for the new bicycle he wanted, but now, staring at his empty table under the hot sun, doubt crept in heavily alongside his nervousness. What if nobody stopped at all? What if his lemonade tasted bad and people drove away without even trying it? He fidgeted with his hand-painted sign, worrying that his lettering looked messy and unprofessional compared to the lemonade stands he had seen other kids run with neat, store-bought signs. Thirty more minutes passed without a single customer, and Теодор's nervousness deepened into something closer to quiet despair, certain that his very first business attempt was going to be a complete and humiliating failure. He considered packing everything up early rather than sitting out here any longer feeling foolish and ignored by every car that passed without even slowing down. Just as he reached for the pitcher to begin packing up, an elderly woman from down the street approached on her daily walk, pausing at his table with genuine interest, asking how much a cup cost. Теодор's hands trembled slightly as he poured her a cup, nervously explaining his recipe included a bit of fresh mint from his mother's garden, and she took a sip, declaring it the best lemonade she had tasted all summer. She bought a second cup to bring home to her husband and mentioned the stand to a neighbor walking by moments later, who also stopped to try a cup for himself. Word seemed to spread in small, steady ripples down the street, and within an hour, Теодор found himself genuinely busy, pouring cup after cup for a small but steady stream of customers, his earlier nervousness fading with every satisfied comment about his secret mint ingredient. By the end of the afternoon, his cash box held far more money than he had expected, and his pitcher sat completely empty for the first time all day. He counted his earnings twice just to be sure, grinning at the realization that he had actually succeeded at something he had been so nervous about just hours earlier. Packing up his table that evening, Теодор felt a surging, well-earned pride replace every trace of his earlier doubt, already planning improvements for an even better stand the following weekend. He ran inside to tell his parents every detail, practically bursting with the kind of pride that came from building something entirely on his own, one nervous, successful cup at a time.

prompt: Write a story about a girl who feels worried about her sister's surgery and then relieved.
response: Natalie sat in the hospital waiting room, knees pulled up to her chest, watching the clock above the double doors tick forward with agonizing slowness while her little sister Josie remained somewhere behind those doors undergoing surgery to fix a problem with her heart that the doctors had discovered only a few months earlier. Her parents sat beside her, equally tense, but Natalie felt a particular kind of worry gnawing at her that she could not quite put into words, a fear that something might go wrong during the surgery and that she might never get to finish teaching Josie how to ride a bike like she had promised just last week. Every time the doors opened, her heart leapt into her throat, hoping for news, only to watch other families greet other doctors with their own updates that had nothing to do with Josie at all. She thought about every small argument she had ever had with her little sister, wishing desperately she could take each one back, convinced that somehow those moments mattered more now than they ever had before. The waiting room television played quietly in the background, but Natalie could not focus on anything except the second hand of the wall clock and the doors that remained stubbornly closed. Two hours passed, then three, each additional hour deepening her worry into something closer to dread, her imagination conjuring increasingly frightening possibilities about what such a long surgery might mean. She gripped her mother's hand tightly, both of them sitting in near silence, unable to find words adequate for the fear sitting heavy between them. Finally, after nearly four hours, the doors swung open and Josie's surgeon walked toward them, pulling down his surgical mask, and Natalie's whole body tensed, bracing for whatever news was coming. The surgeon smiled warmly and explained that the surgery had gone exactly as planned, every repair successful, and that Josie was already waking up in recovery, tired but completely stable and expected to make a full recovery. Relief crashed through Natalie so powerfully that her legs nearly buckled beneath her, and she found herself crying and laughing at the same time, the crushing worry of the past four hours dissolving all at once into pure, overwhelming gratitude. Her parents embraced each other and then her, and the whole family hurried down the hallway together to see Josie as soon as the nurses allowed visitors. When Natalie finally saw her little sister's groggy but genuinely smiling face, she squeezed her hand gently, promising again that bike lesson the moment she felt strong enough. Josie mumbled sleepily that she would hold her to it, and Natalie laughed through happy tears, the worry that had consumed her entire afternoon replaced completely by a deep, settled relief that stayed with her all the way home that night.

prompt: Write a story about a fox who feels disappointed about missing a meal and then feels grateful.
response: Vixen the fox crept along the riverbank at dusk, stomach growling after an entire day of failed hunting attempts, the rabbit she had been stalking for nearly twenty minutes finally darting into a burrow just as she lunged, leaving her with nothing but a mouthful of dirt and a deepening sense of disappointment. This was the third failed hunt of the day, and with winter approaching fast, every missed meal felt like a genuine setback rather than simply bad luck, her ribs already visible beneath her thinning autumn coat. She sat back on her haunches at the riverbank, disappointment settling heavily over her as she watched the sun begin sinking lower, knowing that hunting became far more difficult once true darkness fell across the forest. She thought about her den, empty of any stored food, and worried about the long, hungry night ahead with nothing to show for a full day's determined effort. She considered giving up the hunt entirely for the evening, curling up hungry in her den rather than risking injury stumbling around unfamiliar ground in the dark. Just as she turned to head back toward her den, disappointed and discouraged, she noticed a commotion downstream, a family of otters working together to herd fish into a shallow pool along the riverbank, clearly more successful at fishing than Vixen had ever managed to be on her own. One of the otters, an older female named Reed, noticed Vixen watching from the bank and, surprisingly, called out an invitation for her to share in their catch, explaining that otters always caught more fish than their own family could eat in a single sitting anyway. Vixen hesitated, unused to such generosity from animals that were not even her own kind, but her hunger eventually won out over her pride, and she approached cautiously to find a generous portion of fresh fish set aside specifically for her. She ate gratefully, the disappointment of her failed hunts fading with every satisfying bite of fish she had not even had to catch herself. Reed explained that the otter family often shared surplus catches with hungry neighbors along the river, having learned long ago that generosity during lean seasons tended to come back around eventually when their own luck occasionally ran short instead. Vixen left that evening with a full stomach and something unexpected alongside it, a genuine warmth toward neighbors she had barely known existed before tonight. She returned the following week with a plump rabbit she had successfully caught, insisting Reed's family take a share in return, beginning an ongoing friendship built on generous exchanges between otter and fox. The disappointment of her failed hunting day had led, unexpectedly, to a grateful new friendship and a lesson about community that carried her through the harder hunting days still ahead that winter.

prompt: Write a story about a boy who feels embarrassed during a school play and then feels accepted.
response: Oliver stood frozen center stage during the school play, horrified to feel his oversized costume tree trunk slipping sideways just as he delivered his only line, the whole leafy costume toppling over his head and leaving him standing in front of the entire auditorium wearing nothing but his regular clothes underneath, the tree costume crumpled uselessly around his ankles. A wave of laughter rippled through the audience, and Oliver's face burned redder than he thought possible, certain in that single humiliating moment that he had just ruined the entire play in front of every parent, teacher, and classmate watching. He wanted desperately to run offstage and hide somewhere no one could find him, his mind racing through every terrible thought about how this moment would follow him for the rest of the school year. He fumbled to pick the costume back up, hands shaking, unable to remember his next line even though he had practiced it perfectly dozens of times at home. The stage lights suddenly felt impossibly bright and exposing, and Oliver stood there, frozen and humiliated, certain the entire play was now ruined because of his clumsy mistake. His scene partner, a girl named Beatrice playing the woodland fairy, could have simply continued on without him, but instead she improvised smoothly, declaring loudly in character that even trees sometimes needed to stretch their roots and shake off their leaves for a moment. The audience laughed again, but this time warmly, delighted by her quick thinking rather than mocking Oliver's mistake, and several kids backstage began clapping along playfully. Oliver, catching on to her rescue, quickly refitted his fallen costume and delivered his line late but clearly, and the play continued smoothly from there as if the mishap had simply been part of the performance all along. Backstage after the show, Oliver braced himself for teasing from his castmates, certain they must be frustrated with him for nearly ruining their hard work. Instead, his classmates crowded around laughing good-naturedly about the falling tree costume, several of them admitting their own small mistakes during the performance that the audience had barely noticed at all. Beatrice told him his stunned expression after the costume fell had actually been the funniest and most memorable part of the entire play, meant with genuine affection rather than mockery. His director even praised the unplanned moment for bringing the loudest, warmest laughter of the whole evening. The heavy embarrassment that had gripped Oliver on stage slowly eased into a relieved, grateful feeling of being fully accepted by a cast who clearly liked him regardless of a wardrobe malfunction. He left the auditorium that night laughing along with everyone else about his fallen tree costume, already looking forward to next year's play without a trace of the dread he had expected to feel.

prompt: Write a story about a girl who feels nervous and confused during a science fair and then becomes proud.
response: Ximena stood beside her tri-fold poster board in the crowded school gymnasium, watching judges move slowly from table to table, her stomach twisting into nervous knots as she realized her volcano demonstration looked embarrassingly simple compared to the elaborate robotics project and computer coded game displayed at the tables on either side of her. She had worked hard on her project about chemical reactions, but standing here now, surrounded by so many impressive displays, nervousness crept through her entire body, convinced the judges would barely glance at her modest baking soda volcano before moving on to something more impressive. When the first judge finally arrived at her table and began asking detailed questions about the specific chemical reaction occurring inside her volcano, Ximena found herself growing confused halfway through her answer, stumbling over the scientific terms she thought she had memorized perfectly the night before. The judge asked a follow up question about reaction rates that Ximena had not fully anticipated, and she felt her confidence crumble further, mixing her nervousness with a frustrating confusion about concepts she suddenly worried she did not actually understand as well as she believed. She glanced nervously at the robotics table nearby, where confident explanations flowed easily from the student presenting, and felt increasingly certain that her own project simply did not measure up. The judge thanked her politely and moved on, leaving Ximena standing there feeling both nervous and confused, uncertain whether she had explained anything correctly at all. During a quiet moment between judge visits, her science teacher Mrs. Alvarez stopped by and noticed her clearly shaken expression, asking gently what was wrong. Ximena admitted her confusion about the reaction rate question, and Mrs. Alvarez, instead of simply giving her the answer, walked her through the concept slowly using her own volcano model as a visual example, showing exactly how temperature affected the speed of her chemical reaction in terms Ximena finally understood clearly. Armed with this clearer understanding, Ximena felt something shift inside her chest, nervousness and confusion both settling into a steadier, more confident calm. When the final judge arrived at her table minutes later and asked a similar question, Ximena explained the reaction rate concept clearly and confidently, even demonstrating it live by trying her volcano with slightly warmer vinegar to show the faster reaction in real time. The judge's eyebrows raised with genuine interest, impressed by her hands-on demonstration and clear understanding. When award results were announced that afternoon, Ximena was stunned to hear her name called for best demonstration of scientific concept, beating out several of the more elaborate looking projects she had been so nervous about earlier. The confusion and nervousness that had gripped her for most of the afternoon transformed into an overwhelming, well-earned pride as she walked up to accept her ribbon, proof that genuine understanding mattered more than how impressive a project merely looked from the outside.

prompt: Write a story about a boy whose dog goes missing and who feels scared, then sad, and finally happy when they are reunited.
response: Tobias ran up and down the street as evening fell, calling his dog Scout's name over and over, his voice growing hoarse with a fear that twisted tighter in his chest with every empty yard and silent corner he checked. Scout had slipped through a gap in the fence that afternoon while Tobias was distracted inside, and now, hours later, there was still no sign of him anywhere in the neighborhood, no answering bark, no familiar wagging tail bounding around a corner. Panic gripped Tobias as he imagined Scout lost on busy streets, frightened and alone somewhere he had never explored before, unable to find his way home without help. He and his dad searched for hours with flashlights as darkness fully settled over the neighborhood, checking under porches, behind sheds, and along the creek where Scout loved to wander, but every search came up empty, deepening Tobias's fear into something heavier and more hopeless with each passing hour. By the time they returned home near midnight, exhausted and without any sign of Scout, Tobias's fear had transformed into a deep, aching sadness, convinced that his best friend was gone for good, lost somewhere in the dark where Tobias could not reach him. He lay awake most of the night, picturing Scout's empty dog bed in the corner of his room, tears soaking into his pillow as he imagined mornings without Scout's familiar nose nudging him awake. The following morning, he and his dad printed flyers with Scout's photo, Tobias's hands shaking as he taped them to lamp posts around the neighborhood, sadness weighing down every step as he fought to hold onto even the smallest hope that someone might recognize his missing dog. Hours passed without a single phone call, and Tobias's sadness deepened into a quiet, exhausted grief by midafternoon, certain the flyers had been a hopeless effort. Just as the sun began setting on the second day, the phone rang, and Tobias's mother answered, her face breaking into relieved surprise as she listened to the caller. A family three streets over explained they had found a friendly, exhausted dog matching Scout's description curled up in their garage that morning, too shy and tired to approach anyone until they finally coaxed him out with food. Tobias and his dad rushed over immediately, and the moment Tobias saw Scout's familiar face peek out from behind the family's recycling bins, pure overwhelming joy crashed through him, replacing two full days of fear and sadness all at once. Scout bounded toward him, tail wagging wildly, and Tobias dropped to his knees, wrapping his arms around his dog and burying his face in his fur, laughing and crying at the same time. They walked home together that evening, Scout trotting happily beside him on a firmly held leash, and Tobias could not stop smiling the entire way, grateful beyond words to have his best friend back safe and sound.

prompt: Write a story about a horse who feels embarrassed after stumbling in a race and then feels accepted.
response: Comet the horse thundered down the final stretch of the county fair race, neck and neck with the favored chestnut mare, when his hoof caught an uneven patch of dirt and he stumbled hard, nearly going down completely before scrambling back upright and finishing dead last, far behind every other horse in the race. The crowd's gasps followed by scattered laughter from a few rowdy spectators rang in his ears as he trotted shakily toward the paddock, head hanging low, certain he had just humiliated himself and his young rider in front of the entire fairground. His rider, a girl named Petra, patted his neck gently, but Comet could only think about the stumble, replaying the moment over and over as grooms from other stables glanced his way with what he was sure were pitying or mocking expressions. He refused his usual post-race treats, standing miserably in the corner of his stall, ears pinned back, unwilling to even look toward the stall door where other horses occasionally passed by on their way to the water trough. He overheard, or thought he overheard, two grooms chuckling near his stall, and the embarrassment deepened into something closer to shame, convinced his reputation at the fairground was now permanently ruined. He stayed curled in the corner of his stall long after the race results were posted, refusing to acknowledge Petra when she returned that evening to check on him. The next morning, Petra led him out to the practice ring anyway, and Comet braced himself for more pitying looks from the other horses and riders gathered there. Instead, an old gelding named Duke ambled over and mentioned, without any judgment in his voice, that he had taken a tumble in nearly the exact same spot three years earlier during his very first fair race, the uneven dirt patch apparently notorious among horses who had run that track for years. Two younger horses chimed in with their own stumbling stories, one admitting she had once tripped over her own front hooves crossing the finish line in dead last place the year before. Comet listened, surprised, as story after story emerged, each one met with easy laughter rather than mockery, making clear that stumbles on that particular track happened to nearly everyone eventually. Petra scratched behind his ears and reminded him that he had still fought to finish the race instead of giving up entirely after the stumble, something she considered far more impressive than a perfect, uneventful run. The heavy embarrassment that had gripped Comet since the race finally eased, replaced by a warm, settled feeling of belonging among horses who clearly respected him regardless of one bad stumble. By the following week's practice, Comet trotted confidently past that same uneven patch of dirt, no longer dreading it, accepted fully by a stable that valued his effort far more than a single misstep.

prompt: Write a story about a duckling who feels jealous of a new sibling and then becomes content.
response: Quacker the duckling watched sourly from the edge of the pond as every visiting goose and heron stopped to coo over his brand new baby sister, the tiniest, fluffiest duckling the pond had seen all season, while he paddled around mostly unnoticed nearby. Just weeks ago, he had been the center of attention himself, the youngest and most adored duckling in the family, but now it seemed like every kind word and gentle nuzzle from his mother went straight to his new sister instead. He sulked near the reeds, refusing to join his siblings in their usual games of chase through the shallows, a hot, uncomfortable jealousy twisting in his chest every time his mother tucked his baby sister protectively under her wing. At dinner, when a passing swan commented on how adorable the newest addition to the family was, Quacker paddled away in a huff, muttering to himself about how nobody seemed to notice him anymore at all. He spent the following days drifting at the edges of the family, watching his jealousy grow heavier with every compliment directed at his tiny sister, convinced he had been replaced entirely in his mother's affections. One blustery afternoon, a sudden gust of wind sent his baby sister tumbling off the muddy bank and into a fast-moving current near the pond's outlet, her tiny legs no match for the pulling water sweeping her quickly downstream. Quacker, closer to the current than anyone else, reacted instantly, paddling harder than he ever had in his life, instinct overriding his jealousy completely as he raced to catch up with his struggling sister. He reached her just before the current swept her past a dangerous drop near the old mill wheel, nudging her firmly toward a calm eddy near the bank where his mother, frantic, finally caught up and scooped her to safety. His mother nuzzled him gratefully, praising his quick thinking in front of the entire gathered family, calling him the bravest and most watchful big brother on the whole pond. His baby sister, once she stopped trembling, waddled over and pressed close against him, clearly looking up to him now with obvious admiration. Quacker realized, feeling her small body pressed trustingly against his side, that being a big brother came with its own kind of importance that no amount of cooing attention toward his sister could ever replace. The jealousy that had followed him for days finally settled into a quiet, warm contentment, and from that afternoon forward, he swam proudly beside his little sister everywhere she went, no longer measuring his mother's love in comparisons, simply content in the steady place he held within his own family.

prompt: Write a story about a badger who feels scared during a flood and then becomes brave.
response: Grubwood the badger woke to the alarming sound of rushing water, his burrow already ankle deep and rising fast after days of relentless rain had finally overwhelmed the nearby stream, sending a flash flood pouring directly into the tunnel system his family called home. Panic gripped him instantly as he realized his two young cubs were still asleep in the deepest chamber of the burrow, the one lowest to the ground and therefore most likely to flood first and fastest. He splashed through the rising water, his heart pounding with a fear unlike anything he had felt before, calling out to his cubs over the growing roar of water pouring in through collapsed tunnel walls behind him. The water reached his chest by the time he found them, confused and frightened, paddling weakly in the flooding chamber, and for one terrible moment, Grubwood feared the rising current might separate them before he could reach them at all. Every instinct screamed at him to simply grab the nearest cub and flee toward any exit, fear clouding his thinking as water continued pouring in from multiple directions at once. He forced himself to think clearly despite the terror gripping his chest, remembering an old escape tunnel his own father had shown him years ago, one that led upward toward higher ground rather than deeper into the flooding warren. Fighting against the current, he gathered both trembling cubs against his sides, pushing them firmly toward the upward tunnel while the water continued rising dangerously behind them. The climb was slow and difficult, his cubs slipping repeatedly on the muddy slope, but Grubwood stayed close behind them the entire way, pushing and guiding despite his own exhaustion and the cold water soaking through his fur. They finally emerged onto a rocky hillside above the flooding valley, gasping and soaked but completely safe, watching in stunned silence as water continued rushing through the now completely submerged burrow entrance below them. His cubs pressed close against him, shivering, and Grubwood wrapped his body protectively around them, the fear that had gripped him completely during the climb slowly settling into a steady, relieved calm now that they were safe. When dawn broke and the flood waters finally began receding, Grubwood led his cubs to a dry hollow beneath a fallen tree, where they would stay until a new burrow could be dug on higher ground. His cubs told everyone who would listen in the following days how their father had bravely led them to safety through the rushing floodwaters, and Grubwood, though he still remembered every terrified heartbeat of that climb, carried with him a new quiet confidence that he could protect his family through whatever danger came, having proven it to himself when it mattered most.

prompt: Write a story about a boy who feels confused about a new baby sibling and then comes to understand his new role.
response: Mateo stood in the doorway of the nursery, staring at the tiny, red-faced baby sleeping in the crib that used to be his own room's reading corner, utterly confused about why everything in his house had changed so suddenly and so completely in just one week. His parents seemed exhausted all the time now, constantly distracted by feeding schedules and diaper changes, and Mateo could not understand why this small, mostly sleeping baby required so much more attention than he remembered needing himself, or at least more attention than he currently seemed to be getting. He wandered through the house feeling oddly displaced, uncertain where he fit into this new arrangement where conversations used to be about his school day and now seemed to revolve entirely around the baby's naps and feedings. He asked his mother several confused questions throughout the week, why the baby cried so much, why everyone whispered around her, why his usual Saturday pancake breakfast with his dad had been replaced by his dad bouncing the baby anxiously in the kitchen instead. Each answer left him with more questions than before, a persistent confusion settling over him about what exactly his own role was supposed to be in this suddenly rearranged family. He wondered, without quite admitting it out loud, whether he still mattered as much now that there was a new baby who seemed to need so much more than he apparently did. One evening, his exhausted mother, noticing his quiet, confused mood for days, sat down with him on the couch and asked gently what was bothering him. Mateo admitted everything, the confusion about the schedule changes, the uncertainty about his place in the family, even his quiet worry that he mattered less now. His mother pulled him close and explained patiently that the baby needed so much attention right now simply because she could not yet do anything for herself, not because anyone loved Mateo any less, and that actually, she needed his help more than ever, since an older brother's steady presence meant more to a new baby than almost anything else in the world. She asked if he wanted to help give the baby her evening bottle that very night, carefully guiding his hands as he held her for the very first time. Mateo felt something shift as his baby sister's tiny fingers curled around his own, her eyes blinking up at him with obvious, trusting attention. The confusion that had followed him all week finally settled into a clear, warm understanding of exactly where he belonged in this new family shape. Over the following weeks, Mateo took on small jobs proudly, singing to her during fussy evenings and showing her his favorite toys, no longer confused about his place but confident in his new, important role as her big brother.

prompt: Write a story about a bat that starts out scary in a dark cave and ends up happy.
response: Flicker the young bat had become separated from his colony during a confusing midnight flight through unfamiliar passages, and now he clung upside down to a cold stone ceiling deep within a cave system he had never explored before, every echo bouncing strangely off walls he could not see in the total darkness surrounding him. Strange dripping sounds echoed from somewhere far below, and the air smelled thick and unfamiliar, nothing like the cozy, crowded roost where his entire colony usually gathered each night. He called out using his echolocation clicks, but the chamber's confusing shape sent the sound bouncing back in distorted, unfamiliar patterns that made it impossible to judge how large the space around him truly was, or what might be hiding within it. Every rustle of his own wings against the stone sent jolts of fear through his small body, convinced something unknown shared this dark cavern with him, something large enough to make the air itself feel heavier and more dangerous. He pressed himself flatter against the ceiling, wings wrapped tight around his body, too frightened to attempt flying further into the unknown darkness stretching endlessly in every direction. Hours seemed to pass in that frozen, terrified stillness, the cave's cold damp air settling into his fur as he strained his senses for any sign of his colony or any safe way back toward the entrance he could no longer locate. Just as despair began creeping in alongside his fear, he noticed a faint vibration traveling through the stone itself, rhythmic and familiar, the unmistakable pattern of dozens of bats calling together in their communal roosting song. Hope flickered through his fear, and he launched off the ceiling, following the vibration through passage after unfamiliar passage, the sound growing steadily clearer and louder with every careful, echolocating turn he made. He rounded a final bend and burst into a massive, warm chamber alive with the fluttering wings and soft chattering calls of hundreds of bats clustered together along the ceiling, a sight so welcoming after his frightening isolation that he nearly cried out with relief. His own colony, having also become disoriented in the unfamiliar cave system, had settled here to wait out the confusion, and several bats immediately called out greetings as he landed among them, delighted to see a missing colony member returned safely. Flicker nestled into the warm, crowded cluster of familiar bodies, the fear that had gripped him for hours melting away completely into pure, relieved happiness at being surrounded by his family again. The cave that had seemed so frightening and vast in his isolation now felt simply like an unfamiliar room in an otherwise wonderful, enormous home shared with everyone he loved. From that night forward, Flicker explored new cave passages eagerly alongside his colony, no longer afraid of getting lost, confident that familiar, happy sounds were always somewhere nearby waiting to guide him home.

prompt: Write a story about a girl who feels sad about her family's old house being sold and then becomes hopeful.
response: Lydia walked slowly through the empty rooms of her grandparents' old farmhouse one last time, running her fingers along the worn kitchen counter where she had helped bake cookies every summer visit since she could remember, the realization that the house had just been sold to strangers settling over her like a cold, heavy blanket. Her grandparents had decided they could no longer manage the big old house on their own, and though she understood the reasons, standing in these familiar rooms for what would be the final time made a deep sadness well up in her chest that she could not quite push down. She trailed her hand along the staircase banister worn smooth by generations of family hands, thinking about every holiday dinner, every summer afternoon chasing fireflies in the backyard, every single memory tied so completely to this particular house that she could not imagine her family's history continuing anywhere else. The moving truck outside had already carried away most of her grandparents' furniture, leaving the rooms echoing and strange, stripped of the warmth and clutter that had always made this house feel so alive and loved. She sat on the bare floor of what used to be the upstairs reading nook, tears slipping down her cheeks as she thought about strangers moving in soon, repainting walls, replacing the creaky floorboards she had memorized the sound of, erasing every trace of her family that had ever lived there. Her grandmother found her there and sat down beside her quietly, wrapping an arm around her shoulders without saying anything for a long moment, letting Lydia's sadness simply exist without rushing to fix it. Eventually, her grandmother pulled out an old photo album from a box nearby, one she had saved specifically to look through together before leaving the house for good, filled with decades of photographs taken in every room they currently sat within. She explained that while the house itself would belong to someone new now, every memory captured in these photographs, and every memory living inside Lydia's own heart, belonged entirely and permanently to their family, untouchable by whoever moved in next. She mentioned that her own new smaller house nearby had a garden plot waiting, and that she hoped Lydia would help her plant the very same variety of tomatoes they had grown together in the farmhouse garden every summer, continuing the tradition in a new place instead of ending it here. Lydia looked through photograph after photograph, laughing through her remaining tears at pictures of herself as a toddler covered in flour in that very kitchen. The heavy sadness in her chest slowly made room for something lighter and more hopeful, a growing excitement about helping create new memories with her grandparents in their next chapter together. Walking out of the farmhouse for the final time, Lydia held the photo album tightly against her chest, already looking forward to planting tomatoes in a new garden that coming spring.

prompt: Write a story about a girl in a wheelchair who feels lonely and then becomes joyful at a dance class.
response: Esperanza sat near the back of the community center room, watching a line of girls practicing pirouettes across the wooden dance floor, her wheelchair parked carefully to the side where the instructor had suggested she simply observe for now since the studio had never had a dancer like her before. She had loved dance her entire life, watching videos at home and moving her upper body to the music whenever she could, but every dance class she had tried to join treated her more like a spectator than an actual participant, leaving her to watch from the sidelines while classmates twirled and leaped across floors she could never fully join. The loneliness of sitting apart from the group settled over her familiarly, an ache she had grown almost used to but never quite accepted, watching other girls laugh together during partner exercises that never seemed designed with her in mind. After class, she wheeled herself out to the parking lot alone, her mother asking how it went, and Esperanza simply shrugged, saying it was fine, though privately she wondered whether she would ever find a dance class that actually wanted her fully involved rather than politely included from a distance. The following week, a new instructor named Ms. Odalys arrived, having previously taught adaptive dance programs at another studio across town, and she approached Esperanza directly before class even began, asking detailed questions about what movements felt comfortable and exciting for her specifically. Instead of suggesting Esperanza simply watch, Ms. Odalys spent the first fifteen minutes of class demonstrating wheelchair-based turns and arm sequences that could be performed in perfect unison with the standing dancers' choreography, adjusting the full routine so that every single dancer, standing or seated, moved together as one cohesive group. Esperanza practiced the adapted turns hesitantly at first, unsure her chair could move the way Ms. Odalys described, but found herself spinning smoothly across the floor alongside her classmates for the very first time in her life, genuinely part of the formation instead of watching it from outside. The other girls cheered when she landed a particularly tricky spin sequence, several of them asking afterward if she could show them how she managed to turn so sharply in her chair. By the end of class, Esperanza was laughing harder than she had in months, fully immersed in choreography built specifically to include her as an equal dancer rather than an afterthought. The deep loneliness that had followed her through every previous dance class dissolved completely into a bright, bubbling joy as she realized she had finally found a place where dance truly belonged to her too. She wheeled out to the parking lot that evening practically glowing, telling her mother excitedly about every single turn, already counting down the days until the next class where she could dance, fully and joyfully, among friends who saw her as exactly the dancer she had always been.

prompt: Write a story about a lion cub who feels angry after a failed hunt and then learns to feel calm.
response: Kito the lion cub stalked back toward the pride's resting rock, fur bristling with frustration after watching the gazelle he had been stalking for nearly ten minutes bound away effortlessly the moment he pounced too early, alerting the entire herd before he even got close enough to have a real chance. This was his fourth failed hunting attempt that week, and the anger burning through his small body felt sharper and hotter each time, especially after his older cousin had successfully brought down a hare just that morning with seemingly effortless skill. He swatted irritably at a clump of dry grass, growling under his breath about how unfair it felt that hunting seemed to come so easily to every other cub in the pride except him. When his cousin asked cheerfully about his hunt, Kito snapped back sharply, stalking away before the conversation could continue, his anger making him want to be anywhere except around other cubs who seemed to succeed so effortlessly at something he kept failing. He spent the rest of the afternoon alone at the edge of the pride's territory, replaying his pounce over and over in frustrated anger, convinced that something was simply wrong with him that no amount of practice would ever fix. His mother found him there as the sun began setting, noticing his bristled fur and irritated pacing, and settled down calmly beside him without immediately asking what was wrong. After a long silence, she mentioned that she herself had failed nearly every hunt during her first full season as a young lioness, pouncing too early almost every single time out of sheer overeager excitement, much like Kito's pounce that morning. Kito looked at her skeptically, struggling to imagine his graceful, successful mother ever failing at anything related to hunting. She explained that patience, not speed or strength, was the single hardest and most important skill any young hunter had to learn, and that his anger after each failed attempt was actually making him pounce even earlier out of frustrated impatience, creating exactly the mistake that kept costing him his hunts. She suggested that calm, controlled breathing before each pounce had eventually fixed her own overeager tendencies, more than any amount of frustrated anger ever could have. Kito sat with her words for a long moment, feeling the hot anger in his chest slowly begin to settle as he considered her explanation honestly for the first time. The following morning, he approached a young hare in the tall grass, forcing himself to breathe slowly and wait despite every impatient instinct urging him to pounce immediately. When the perfect moment finally arrived, he struck calmly and precisely, catching the hare on his very first patient attempt of the week. The anger that had consumed him for days dissolved into a quiet, steady pride, and Kito carried that same patient calm into every hunt afterward, remembering exactly how much more effective calm had been than fury.

prompt: Write a story about a boy who feels worried about his new puppy's vet visit and then feels relieved.
response: Sammy sat in the cold plastic chair of the veterinary clinic waiting room, clutching his new puppy Biscuit's leash tightly, worry twisting in his stomach after noticing that Biscuit had been unusually quiet and tired all morning, refusing even his favorite breakfast treat. He had only had Biscuit for two short weeks, barely enough time to learn all his puppy habits, and the sudden change in behavior had sent his parents rushing him straight to the emergency vet appointment instead of waiting for his scheduled checkup next month. Sammy watched other pets being called back one by one, each passing minute stretching his worry tighter, imagining every possible terrible reason Biscuit might be feeling so unwell so soon after joining their family. He thought about how attached he had already become in just two weeks, teaching Biscuit to sit, letting him sleep curled against his feet every night, and the thought of something seriously wrong with his new best friend made his chest ache with a fear he had never quite felt before. When the veterinary technician finally called Biscuit's name, Sammy's legs felt shaky as he carried the unusually still puppy back toward the examination room, his parents following close behind with equally worried expressions. The veterinarian, a kind older woman named Dr. Osei, examined Biscuit thoroughly, checking his temperature, his belly, and his energy levels while Sammy stood by gripping his father's hand tightly, bracing for bad news with every passing silent minute. Dr. Osei asked several questions about what Biscuit had eaten recently, and Sammy's mother mentioned, almost as an afterthought, that they had given him a new brand of puppy treats just yesterday for the first time. Dr. Osei nodded knowingly and explained that Biscuit's symptoms matched a simple, common reaction some puppies had to switching food too quickly, nothing serious or dangerous at all, just an upset stomach that would resolve within a day or two with some bland food and rest. Relief flooded through Sammy so suddenly and completely that he felt almost dizzy with it, the heavy worry that had gripped him all morning dissolving instantly into grateful, lightheaded happiness. Dr. Osei recommended a simple diet of plain rice and chicken for the next two days, assuring them that Biscuit's energy would likely return to its usual bouncy self by tomorrow. Sammy scooped Biscuit up carefully, hugging him gently, already noticing the puppy seemed to perk up slightly just from the reassurance in the room. On the drive home, Biscuit sat happily in Sammy's lap, nudging his hand for attention exactly like his normal energetic self, and by the next afternoon, he was back to chasing his favorite squeaky toy across the living room floor. Sammy never again switched his puppy's food without checking carefully first, grateful beyond words that his worried morning had ended in nothing more than a simple, easily fixed lesson learned.

prompt: Write a story about a mouse who feels disappointed about a small house and then becomes grateful.
response: Pip the mouse scurried through the walls of the old farmhouse, peering enviously through a crack at the grand, elaborate mouse den that his cousin Squeak had built beneath the pantry floorboards, complete with multiple rooms, soft cotton bedding, and a pantry entrance offering easy access to crumbs of every delicious variety. His own home, a single small burrow tucked beneath the back porch steps, suddenly felt embarrassingly plain and cramped by comparison, barely large enough for one simple sleeping nook and nowhere near the pantry's convenient treasures. He spent an entire afternoon visiting his cousin's elaborate den, admiring every clever tunnel and storage room, returning to his own modest burrow afterward with a heavy disappointment settling over him at how small and unimpressive his home truly was. He complained to his mother that evening, insisting their burrow was practically an embarrassment compared to Squeak's impressive pantry den, wishing desperately they could move somewhere grander and more convenient. His mother listened patiently but did not immediately argue, simply nodding along as Pip listed every disappointing comparison between their modest burrow and his cousin's elaborate one. That very night, a sudden commotion erupted from beneath the pantry floorboards, frantic squeaking and scrambling sounds echoing through the farmhouse walls as the household cat, having discovered the pantry den's convenient entrance, began pawing furiously at the floorboards trying to reach the mice hiding inside. Pip and his mother listened in alarm as Squeak's entire family came racing through the wall tunnels in a desperate panic, having narrowly escaped the cat's claws by fleeing through their den's elaborate but ultimately exposed pantry entrance. Squeak's family spent the rest of that frightening night crowded uncomfortably into Pip's small, plain burrow beneath the porch steps, the only truly safe hiding spot nearby, tucked far from any cat-accessible entrance and protected by thick, solid porch boards above. Squeak admitted shakily, pressed into the cramped space, that he had never once considered how exposed his impressive pantry entrance actually left his family until tonight's terrifying encounter. Pip realized, looking around at his own small but genuinely secure burrow now crowded with grateful relatives, that the modest home he had been disappointed in just hours earlier had actually kept his family completely safe from the exact danger that had nearly caught his cousin's elaborate one. The disappointment he had carried all evening transformed into a deep, settled gratitude for his simple, sturdy little burrow, which suddenly felt like the finest and safest home in the entire farmhouse walls. From that night forward, Pip never once complained about his small burrow again, and Squeak's family eventually moved their den to a spot just as safely hidden, inspired entirely by the humble little burrow that had sheltered them when it mattered most.

prompt: Write a story about a girl who feels nervous and scared during a talent show but ends up feeling proud.
response: Rosalind stood backstage at the community talent show, peeking through a gap in the curtain at the packed auditorium, her violin trembling slightly in her grip as nervousness and genuine fear tangled together in her chest at the thought of performing the difficult solo piece she had been practicing for months. She had never played in front of more than her immediate family before, and the size of the crowd, combined with the bright stage lights she could see flooding the stage beyond the curtain, sent a cold wave of fear through her entire body. Her hands felt clammy against the violin's neck, and she worried that her fingers, usually so steady during practice at home, might shake too badly to play the fast, difficult passage near the end of her piece. She watched the performer ahead of her finish a magic trick to warm applause and felt her stomach drop as the stage manager whispered that she was next, gently guiding her toward the curtain's edge. For one terrifying moment, genuine panic gripped her, and she seriously considered telling the stage manager she had changed her mind, that she could not possibly walk out onto that stage in front of so many watching eyes. Her legs felt locked in place, fear and nervousness combining into something that made even breathing feel difficult, and she squeezed her eyes shut, picturing every way the performance could go wrong in front of the entire audience. The announcer called her name, and the curtain began to part, leaving her no more time to retreat even if she wanted to. Forcing one foot in front of the other, she walked out onto the stage on legs that felt barely her own, the bright lights making the audience disappear into a blur of indistinct shapes rather than individual judging faces. She lifted her violin with trembling hands, and as she drew her first note, something in the familiar motion of her own bow steadied her shaking fingers just slightly. She focused entirely on the music itself instead of the crowd, exactly as her teacher had always coached her to do, letting muscle memory from months of practice carry her through the piece's challenging opening measures. By the time she reached the difficult fast passage near the end, her fear had narrowed into pure concentration, her fingers finding each note with a precision that surprised even her. She drew her final note and held it, the auditorium bursting into enthusiastic applause the moment she lowered her bow. Walking offstage on legs still slightly shaky, Rosalind felt an overwhelming, disbelieving pride replace every trace of her earlier fear and nervousness, hardly able to believe she had actually performed the entire piece without a single mistake. Her parents met her backstage with proud hugs, and Rosalind realized that facing her fear directly, rather than running from it, had given her one of the proudest moments of her entire life.

prompt: Write a story about a boy who feels guilty after breaking his sister's toy and then feels forgiven.
response: Desmond stared down at the broken pieces of his little sister's favorite stuffed rabbit's music box, the delicate mechanism inside now scattered across his bedroom floor after he had taken it apart that afternoon simply to see how the music worked, never intending to actually break it beyond repair. The guilt hit him immediately and heavily as he tried unsuccessfully to fit the tiny gears back together, realizing with growing dread that he had no idea how to reassemble something so delicate and that his sister Ruby cherished this particular toy more than anything else she owned, a gift from their late grandmother that played her favorite lullaby every time it was wound. He hid the broken pieces in his desk drawer, hoping somehow the problem would resolve itself, though deep down he knew Ruby would notice the moment she reached for her beloved rabbit that evening before bed. Sure enough, her confused, searching cries echoed from her room within the hour, and Desmond's guilt swelled into something closer to dread as he heard her ask their mother where her rabbit had gone. He avoided both of them for the rest of the evening, eating dinner in near silence, unable to meet Ruby's eyes across the table, the guilty weight in his stomach making it difficult to swallow even his favorite meal. That night, lying awake, he finally could not bear the guilt any longer and crept to Ruby's room, where he found her sniffling quietly into her pillow, clearly having searched everywhere for her missing toy. He confessed everything in a rush, pulling the broken pieces from his pocket and explaining through his own threatening tears that he had only wanted to understand how the music worked and had never meant to break something so special to her. Ruby's tears turned briefly sharper with hurt and anger, and Desmond braced himself for her to never forgive him, certain he had ruined something precious that could never truly be replaced. Their mother, overhearing the confession, suggested they bring the broken music box to a toy repair shop downtown the following weekend, explaining that such mechanisms, while delicate, were often repairable by someone with the right tools and patience. Ruby considered this through her remaining tears, and slowly, her anger softened into cautious hope at the possibility of hearing her grandmother's lullaby again. The following Saturday, the repair shop owner carefully reassembled the tiny mechanism, and when Ruby wound the key with trembling hands, the familiar lullaby melody tinkled out clear and perfect, exactly as it always had. She hugged Desmond tightly right there in the shop, telling him she forgave him completely, especially since he had been brave enough to confess instead of letting her wonder forever what happened. The guilt that had consumed Desmond for days dissolved into warm, grateful relief, and he never took apart any of Ruby's toys again without asking first.

prompt: Write a story about a girl who feels embarrassed after singing off key at a recital and then feels accepted.
response: Fatima stood on the small stage of the community music recital, midway through her solo song, when her voice suddenly cracked badly on the highest note, sliding noticeably off key in front of the packed audience of parents and fellow students. Her face flushed hot with embarrassment as she pushed through the remaining lyrics, her voice shaky and unsure for the rest of the performance, painfully aware of every imperfect note that followed the initial mistake. She rushed through her final verse faster than she had rehearsed, eager simply to finish and escape the stage before anyone could focus on her mistake any longer than necessary. When she finished, the polite applause felt, to her ears, more sympathetic than enthusiastic, and she hurried backstage with her cheeks still burning, certain that everyone in the audience was now thinking only of her cracked, off-key note rather than anything else about her performance. She sat alone in the backstage area, refusing to come out even when her music teacher called her name gently, replaying the cracked note over and over in her mind until it felt like the only thing that had happened during her entire performance. Her best friend Priya finally found her there, sitting with her knees pulled up, refusing to make eye contact with anyone who passed by. Priya sat down beside her and admitted that she herself had forgotten an entire verse during her own performance just twenty minutes earlier, having to hum nonsense syllables until the words finally came back to her, a mistake Fatima had not even noticed because she had been too nervous about her own upcoming performance to focus on anyone else's. This surprised Fatima, who had assumed everyone in the audience had been focused entirely on her own mistake rather than their own performances or simply enjoying the overall recital. Slowly, other students began sharing their own small recital mishaps as they gathered backstage, one admitting her sheet music had fallen off the stand mid-song, another confessing he had walked out wearing mismatched socks that his mother had only just pointed out. Fatima found herself laughing along with each story, the hot embarrassment in her chest gradually easing as she realized that small mistakes seemed to happen to nearly every performer at every recital, not just her. Her music teacher found her backstage and praised her specifically for pushing through to finish the song instead of stopping after the cracked note, calling that kind of resilience far more valuable than a single perfect performance. By the time the recital ended and families gathered for refreshments, Fatima found herself laughing and chatting easily with her fellow performers, the embarrassment of her cracked note completely replaced by a warm, settled feeling of belonging among friends who clearly accepted every imperfect note along with every perfect one.

prompt: Write a story about a boy who feels jealous of the attention his new baby sister gets and then becomes content.
response: Carter sat at the kitchen table picking unhappily at his dinner, watching his parents take turns cooing over his new baby sister Willa, who had arrived just three weeks ago and seemed to absorb every spare moment of attention his parents used to spend on him. He remembered when dinner conversations used to center around his school day, his soccer practice, his favorite jokes, but lately every meal seemed to revolve entirely around Willa's feeding schedule, her sleep habits, and how many adorable new sounds she had made that day. A hot, uncomfortable jealousy churned in his stomach every time a relative called just to ask about the new baby without mentioning him at all, or when his grandmother's visit consisted almost entirely of holding Willa while Carter sat quietly on the couch, largely unnoticed. He started acting out in small ways, leaving his toys scattered deliberately across the living room floor, answering questions with short, grumpy responses, anything to pull some fraction of attention back toward himself instead of constantly toward his baby sister. His parents, exhausted from sleepless nights, grew increasingly frustrated with his behavior without fully understanding what was driving it, which only deepened Carter's jealousy and his growing sense that he simply mattered less than he used to in his own family. One evening, his father found him sulking alone in his room and sat down on the edge of his bed, asking directly what had been bothering him so much lately. Carter, after some hesitant resistance, finally admitted the truth, that he felt invisible now that Willa had arrived, as if nobody in the family cared about him the way they used to before she was born. His father listened carefully, then admitted that newborns did require an overwhelming amount of attention simply to survive, but that this intense period would not last forever, and more importantly, that Carter's role as a big brother was something entirely unique that no amount of parental attention toward Willa could ever replace or diminish. He asked if Carter wanted to help give Willa her bath that night, something Carter had never been trusted to help with before. Carefully guided by his father, Carter held his baby sister gently, watching her tiny fingers wrap instinctively around his own thumb, her eyes focusing on his face with what looked remarkably like genuine recognition and interest. Something warm replaced the jealousy sitting in his chest as he realized Willa seemed to light up specifically at his presence in a way she did not quite do for anyone else yet. Over the following weeks, Carter took on more small responsibilities with his sister, singing silly songs that made her giggle, a sound only he seemed able to reliably produce. The jealousy that had gripped him for weeks settled slowly into a proud, quiet contentment, and Carter discovered that being a big brother gave him an important place in the family that had simply been waiting for him to grow into it.
